en: Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga) 1.
The Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya)
The four foundations of mindfulness:

here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, and he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally;
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating mind in mind internally; he dwells contemplating mind in mind externally...
He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally,
and he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally, ardent and clearly comprehending.
Possessing mindfulness, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
1.1. The Exposition of the Contemplation of the Body:
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body internally?
Here, a bhikkhu contemplates his own body upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the hair of the head, enclosed by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys;
heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile..."
“Phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine.
He cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that sign; he defines it as it has been defined.
Having cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced that sign, and having defined it as it has been defined, he applies his mind to the body externally.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body externally?
Here, a bhikkhu reviews the external body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys..."
"The heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; the entrails, mesentery, gorge, dung;
bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, urine.
He cultivates that sign, develops it, makes much of it, and defines it as it has been defined.
Thus, having cultivated that sign, developed it, and made much of it, and having defined it well-defined, he applies his mind to the body internally and externally.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body internally and externally?

Here, a bhikkhu contemplates the body internally and externally, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity: [He reflects: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys; heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; bowels, entrails, gorge, dung; bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine."
“In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys;
heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces;
bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, and urine.”
In this way, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Regarding the term “contemplating”: what therein is contemplation?
That wisdom which is understanding ... [as above] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called "contemplation.
One is endowed with this contemplation, fully endowed, arrived at it, fully arrived at it, possessed of it, perfected in it, and equipped with it.
Therefore it is said, “contemplating.
“Dwells” means:
he moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, sustains, conducts himself, and dwells.
Therefore it is said, "he dwells.
Regarding "ardent":
what therein is ardor?
That which is the mental arousal of energy … [as above] … right effort—this is called "ardor.
By means of this ardor, he is possessed of it, fully possessed of it; he has approached it, fully approached it; he is endowed with it, perfected in it, and equipped with it.
Therefore it is said, "ardent.
Regarding "clearly comprehending":
therein, what is clear comprehension?
That wisdom which is understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—
this is called "clear comprehension. By means of this clear comprehension,
he is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, has approached it, fully approached it, is possessed of it, perfected in it, and is equipped with it.
Therefore it is said, "possessing clear comprehension.
"Possessing mindfulness":
therein, what is mindfulness?
That which is mindfulness, recollection …pe… right mindfulness—
this is called "mindfulness.
One is endowed with this mindfulness, fully endowed, approached, fully approached, attained, perfected, and possessed of it.
Therefore it is said, "possessing mindfulness.
Regarding the phrase, "having removed covetousness and dejection in the world":
therein, what is the world?
This very body is the world.
Also, the five aggregates of clinging are the world.
This is called "the world."
In this context, what is covetousness?
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... infatuation of the mind—this is called "covetousness."
In this context, what is mental grief (*domanassa*)?
That which is mental unease, mental suffering, an unpleasant and painful experience born of mental contact, an unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact—
this is called "mental grief."

Thus, both this covetousness and this displeasure are removed, thoroughly removed, calmed, stilled, subsided, come to an end, utterly vanished, dissolved, completely dissolved, withered away, completely withered away, and brought to an end in this world.
Therefore it is said: "having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
This concludes the description of the contemplation of the body.

1.2. The Exposition of the Contemplation of Feelings (Vedanānupassanāniddesa) And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating feelings in feelings internally? Here, a bhikkhu, experiencing a pleasant feeling, understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling. Experiencing a painful feeling... [he understands: "I am experiencing a painful feeling. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a neutral feeling. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling accompanied by greed. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling free from greed. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a painful feeling accompanied by aversion. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a painful feeling free from aversion. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a neutral feeling accompanied by ignorance. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a neutral feeling free from ignorance. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a worldly pleasant feeling. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a supramundane pleasant feeling. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a worldly painful feeling. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a supramundane painful feeling. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a worldly neutral feeling. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a supramundane neutral feeling. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a feeling that will lead to future birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. ... [he understands: "I am experiencing a feeling that will lead to the cessation of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally.
Experiencing a feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a painful feeling";
experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling";
or, experiencing a sensual pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a sensual pleasant feeling"; or, experiencing a non-sensual pleasant feeling...
When experiencing a feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a non-material pleasant feeling"; or when experiencing a material painful feeling, one understands:
"I am experiencing a material painful feeling"; or when experiencing a non-material painful feeling, one understands:
"I am experiencing a non-material painful feeling"; or [when experiencing] a material neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling...

While experiencing a feeling, he understands: "I am experiencing a worldly feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant," or while experiencing a non-worldly feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he understands: "I am experiencing a non-worldly feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
He cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that sign, and he defines it as it has been defined.
Thus, having cultivated that sign, developed it, and made much of it, and having well-determined it, he applies his mind to external feelings.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating feelings in external feelings?
Here, a bhikkhu, when feeling a pleasant feeling, understands: "I feel a pleasant feeling"; [when feeling] a painful [feeling...]
When feeling a painful feeling, one understands: "I am feeling a painful feeling";
when feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling";
and when feeling a worldly pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am feeling a worldly pleasant feeling," or when feeling an unworldly pleasant feeling...
When experiencing a non-material pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a non-material pleasant feeling";
when experiencing a material painful feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a material painful feeling"; when experiencing a non-material painful feeling, one understands:
"I am experiencing a non-material painful feeling"; or when experiencing a material neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling...

While experiencing a feeling, he understands: "He experiences a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling," or while experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: "He experiences an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that sign, and he defines it as it has been defined.
Having cultivated that sign, developed it, and made much of it, and having well-defined it, he applies his mind to internal and external feelings.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating feelings in feelings internally and externally?
Here, a bhikkhu understands a pleasant feeling as "a pleasant feeling," and a painful feeling as "a painful feeling."
He understands; he understands neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling";
he understands carnal pleasant feeling as "carnal pleasant feeling," or he understands non-carnal pleasant feeling as "non-carnal pleasant feeling";
he understands carnal painful feeling as "carnal painful feeling."
One understands an unworldly painful feeling as "an unworldly painful feeling";

one understands a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as "a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"; and one understands an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as "an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."

In this way, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings as feelings internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Contemplating” … [as before] … “dwells” … [as before].
“Exerting himself,” … “clearly comprehending,” … “mindful,” … [and so forth] … “possessing mindfulness.”
“Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
In this context, what is the world?
That very feeling is the world.
The five aggregates of clinging are the world.
This is called "the world.
In this context, what is covetousness?
Whatever lust, infatuation, ...pe... infatuation of the mind—this is called covetousness (*abhijjhā*).
In this context, what is grief (*domanassa*)?
That which is mental unease, mental suffering, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact, the unpleasant and painful sensation born of mental contact— this is called "grief. Thus,

this covetousness and this grief are here in this world disciplined, thoroughly disciplined, stilled, calmed, pacified, subsided, vanished, utterly vanished, dissolved, completely dissolved, withered, completely withered, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: "Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
This is the exposition on the contemplation of feelings. 1.3. Exposition on the Contemplation of the Mind.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the mind as mind internally?
Here, a bhikkhu understands a mind affected by lust as "my mind is affected by lust," or he understands a mind free from lust as "my mind is free from lust";
or he understands a mind affected by hatred as "my mind is affected by hatred."
He understands a mind free from hatred as "my mind is free from hatred"; he understands a deluded mind as "my mind is deluded";
he understands a mind free from delusion as "my mind is free from delusion";
he understands a contracted mind as "my mind is contracted"; he understands a distracted mind as "my mind is distracted."
He understands a mind as "mind"; he understands an exalted mind as "my mind is exalted," or he understands a non-exalted mind as "my mind is not exalted";
he understands a surpassable mind as "my mind is surpassable," or he understands an unsurpassable mind as "my mind is unsurpassable"; or he understands a concentrated mind...
He understands, "My mind is concentrated"; or he understands an unconcentrated mind as, "My mind is unconcentrated";
or he understands a liberated mind as, "My mind is liberated"; or he understands an unliberated mind as, "My mind is unliberated."
Thus he cultivates that sign, develops it, makes much of it, and defines it as it has been defined.
Having cultivated that sign, developed it, made much of it, and defined it as it has been defined, he directs his mind to the mind externally.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the mind in the mind externally?
Here, monks, a monk, if his mind is possessed by lust, understands: "His mind is possessed by lust"; if his mind is free from lust, he understands: "His mind is free from lust.
If his mind is possessed by hatred, he understands: "His mind is possessed by hatred"; if his mind is free from hatred, he understands: "His mind is free from hatred.
If his mind is possessed by delusion... [he understands: "His mind is possessed by delusion"]... [if his mind is free from delusion, he understands: "His mind is free from delusion"].
He understands a mind with delusion as “his mind has delusion”; or he understands a mind free from delusion as “his mind is free from delusion.
He understands a contracted mind as “his mind is contracted”; or he understands a distracted mind as “his mind is distracted.
Or he understands a magnified mind as “his mind is magnified.”
He understands his mind as "the mind"; or he understands his unexalted mind as "his mind is unexalted";
or he understands his surpassable mind as "his mind is surpassable"; or he understands his unsurpassable mind as "his mind is unsurpassable";
or he understands his concentrated mind as "his mind is concentrated."
He understands; he understands his uncomposed mind as "his mind is uncomposed";
he understands his liberated mind as "his mind is liberated"; he understands his unliberated mind as "his mind is unliberated.
He cultivates, develops, and multiplies that sign, and he defines it as well-defined.
Thus, having cultivated that sign, developed it, and made much of it, and having well-defined it, he applies his mind to the mind internally and externally.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the mind as the mind internally and externally?
Here, a bhikkhu understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," or a mind without lust as "a mind without lust."
He understands the mind as "mind"; he understands a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred," or a mind free from hatred as "a mind free from hatred";
he understands a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion," or a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion";
or he understands a contracted mind as "a contracted mind."
He understands; he understands a scattered mind as "a scattered mind";
he understands an exalted mind as "an exalted mind"; he understands an unexalted mind as "an unexalted mind";
he understands a surpassable mind as "a surpassable mind"; he understands an unsurpassable mind as "an unsurpassable mind."

He understands the mind as "mind"; or he understands a concentrated mind as "a concentrated mind," an unconcentrated mind as "an unconcentrated mind," a liberated mind as "a liberated mind," and an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind."
In this way, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind as mind internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Contemplating” … [as before] … “dwells” … [as before].
“Ardent,” ... [and so on] ...
“clearly comprehending,” ... [and so on] ...
“mindful,” ... [and so on] ...
“Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
In this context, what is the world?
That very mind is the world.
The world consists of the five aggregates of clinging.
In this context, what is covetousness?
It is lust, infatuation... [as before] ...infatuation of the mind.
This is called covetousness.
In this context, what is grief?
It is that which is mental unease, mental suffering, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact—that unpleasant and painful sensation born of mental contact.
This is called "mental distress.

Thus, this covetousness and this mental distress are here in this world disciplined, thoroughly disciplined, calmed, stilled, subsided, come to an end, passed away, vanished, dissolved, completely dissolved, exhausted, utterly exhausted, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: "having removed covetousness and mental distress regarding the world."
The Exposition of the Contemplation of Mind.
1.4. The Exposition of the Contemplation of Mental Objects.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating mental objects as mental objects internally?
Here, monks, if sensual desire is present within him, a monk understands: "There is sensual desire in me";
or if sensual desire is not present within him, he understands: "There is no sensual desire in me.
He understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and he understands how there comes to be the abandonment of arisen sensual desire.
There is the abandoning of sensual desire, and he understands that; and he understands how there is the non-arising of abandoned sensual desire in the future.
Or, when ill will is present within him... [and so on].
When there is sloth and torpor within him, he understands: "There is sloth and torpor within me";
when there is restlessness and remorse within him...
when there is doubt within him, he understands: "There is doubt within me"; and when it is not present...
Or, when doubt is present within him, he understands: "There is doubt within me";
and he understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen doubt; and he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen doubt;
and he understands how there comes to be the future non-arising of abandoned doubt.
When the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of mindfulness is present within me";
when the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is not present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of mindfulness is not present within me.
He understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness comes to arise, and he understands how the arisen [enlightenment factor of mindfulness]...
There is fulfillment through the development of the mindfulness enlightenment factor, and he understands that; or, when the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is present within him...
[and so on] ...or, when the energy enlightenment factor is present within him...
[and so on] ...or, when the rapture enlightenment factor is present within him... [and so on].
Or, when the enlightenment factor of tranquility is present within him...
or when the enlightenment factor of concentration is present within him...
or when the enlightenment factor of equanimity is present within him, he knows: "The enlightenment factor of equanimity is present within me."
He understands it; or, if the enlightenment factor of equanimity is not present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of equanimity is not present within me.

He understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the enlightenment factor of equanimity once it has arisen.
Thus he pursues that sign, develops it, cultivates it repeatedly, and defines it as it has been defined.
Having pursued, developed, cultivated that sign, and having defined it as it has been defined, he applies his mind to external phenomena.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in external phenomena?
Here, monks, if sensual desire is present in him, a monk understands: "Sensual desire is present in him";
if sensual desire is not present in him, he understands: "Sensual desire is not present in him.
He also understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen sensual desire.
He understands it, and he understands how the abandoned sensual desire does not arise again in the future.
Or, when ill will is present in him...
or when sloth and torpor are present in him... [and so forth].
When restlessness and remorse have subsided in him...
[and so on] ...or when doubt has subsided in him, he understands: "There is doubt in him"; or when doubt has not subsided in him, he understands:
"There is no doubt in him"; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen doubt.
He understands that, and he understands how the abandoning of arisen doubt occurs;
he understands that, and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned doubt occurs in the future.
Or, when the mindfulness enlightenment factor is present in him, he understands: "The mindfulness enlightenment factor is present in him"; or when it is not present...
He understands, "The enlightenment factor of mindfulness is absent in him," and he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness,
and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness.
Or his factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena being present...
or his factor of enlightenment of energy being present...
or his factor of enlightenment of rapture being present... [and so on].
Or, when his factor of enlightenment of tranquility is present...
[and so on] ...or, when his factor of enlightenment of concentration is present...
[and so on] ...or, when his factor of enlightenment of equanimity is present, he understands: "He has the factor of enlightenment of equanimity"; or, when it is absent...
He understands, "He does not have the enlightenment factor of equanimity," and he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity,
and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity.
Thus he pursues that sign, develops it, cultivates it repeatedly, and defines it as it has been defined.
Having pursued, developed, cultivated it repeatedly, and having defined it as it has been defined, he applies his mind to internal and external phenomena.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena with respect to internal and external phenomena?
Here, a bhikkhu, when sensual desire is present, understands: "Sensual desire is present"; or when sensual desire is absent, he understands:
"Sensual desire is absent. He understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen sensual desire. And how...
And he understands the non-arising in the future of that sensual desire which has been abandoned.
Or, there being ill will...
or, there being sloth and torpor... [and so forth].
When restlessness and remorse are present, he understands, "There is restlessness and remorse";
when doubt is present, he understands, "There is doubt"; and when doubt is absent, he understands, "There is no doubt.
Furthermore, he understands how the arising of unarisen doubt comes about.
He understands how the abandoning of arisen doubt comes about, and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned doubt occurs in the future.

Or, when the mindfulness enlightenment factor is present, he understands, "The mindfulness enlightenment factor is present"; or, when the mindfulness enlightenment factor is absent, [he understands that it is absent].
He understands: "The enlightenment factor of mindfulness does not exist"; he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness;
and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness.
Or, when the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena exists... [and so on].
Or the enlightenment factor of energy that is present …pe… or the enlightenment factor of rapture that is present …pe… or the enlightenment factor of tranquility that is present …pe…
When the enlightenment factor of tranquility is present...
[and so on] ...or when the enlightenment factor of equanimity is present, he understands, "The enlightenment factor of equanimity exists";
or when the enlightenment factor of equanimity is absent, he understands, "The enlightenment factor of equanimity does not exist. And as to how it arises in one in whom it has not yet arisen...

There is the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity, and he understands that; and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment of the development of the enlightenment factor of equanimity once it has arisen.

In this way, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Contemplating.
In this context, what is contemplation?
It is that wisdom, understanding … [as before] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
This is called "contemplation" (*anupassanā*).
One who is endowed with this contemplation— fully endowed, approached, fully approached, attained, perfected, and possessed—
is therefore called "one who contemplates" (*anupassī*).
“Dwells” (*viharati*):
he moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, sustains, conducts himself, and dwells.
Therefore it is said, “he dwells.”
“Exerting himself” (ātāpī).
In this context, what is exertion?
It is the arousal of mental energy … [as before] … right effort.
This is called "ardor.
One who is endowed with this ardor ... [as before] ...
possessed of it, is therefore called "ardent."
“Clearly comprehending.
In this context, what is clear comprehension?
It is wisdom, understanding … [as before] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
This is called "clear comprehension.
One who is endowed with this clear comprehension ... [as above] ... is possessed of it.
Therefore, one is said to be "clearly comprehending."
“Possessing mindfulness.
In this context, what is mindfulness?
That which is mindfulness, recollection … [as above] … right mindfulness.
This is called "mindfulness.
One who is endowed with this mindfulness ... [as before] ... is possessed of it.
Therefore, one is called "mindful."
“Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
In this context, what is the world?
Those very phenomena are the world.
The five aggregates of clinging are the world.
This is called "the world.
In this context, what is covetousness?
Whatever lust, infatuation, ...pe... infatuation of the mind—this is called covetousness (*abhijjhā*).
In this context, what is grief (*domanassa*)?
That which is mental unease, mental suffering, an unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact— an unpleasant and painful sensation born of mental contact— this is called "grief. Thus,

this covetousness and this grief are here in this world disciplined, thoroughly disciplined, calmed, stilled, subsided, come to an end, passed away, vanished, dissolved, completely dissolved, brought to an end, and terminated.
Therefore it is said: "Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
This is the Exposition of the Contemplation of Mental Objects.
The Analysis According to the Discourses (*Suttantabhājanīya*).
2. The Exposition of the Abhidhamma:

The Four Foundations of Mindfulness—here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, and he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna—leading to liberation, leading to the waning of acquisitions—for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna.
He dwells contemplating the body in the body, with a practice that is painful and slow in direct knowledge; whatever at that time is mindfulness, constant mindfulness, right mindfulness,
the mindfulness enlightenment factor, the path factor, included within the path—
this is called "the foundation of mindfulness."
The remaining phenomena are associated with the foundations of mindfulness.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating feelings in feelings?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction of the acquisitions, [freeing him] from views...
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures...
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge, while contemplating feelings in feelings.

Whatever at that time is mindfulness, recollection, right mindfulness, the mindfulness enlightenment factor, a factor of the path, included within the path—that is [the mindfulness enlightenment factor].
This is called "the foundation of mindfulness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the foundation of mindfulness.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the mind in the mind?

Here, monks, at whatever time a monk develops supramundane jhāna that leads out, which goes toward the diminution [of defilements], for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage—being secluded from sensual pleasures ... [as before] ...
having attained the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge, he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind; whatever mindfulness there is at that time...
Mindfulness, right mindfulness, the mindfulness enlightenment factor, the path factor, and that which is included in the path—
this is called "the establishment of mindfulness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the establishment of mindfulness.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna—leading to liberation, leading to the waning of existence—for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...having attained the first jhāna.
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with a difficult practice and sluggish direct knowledge; whatever at that time is mindfulness,
recollection, right mindfulness, the mindfulness enlightenment factor, the path factor, included within the path—
this is called "the foundation of mindfulness."
The remaining phenomena are associated with the foundations of mindfulness.
In that regard, what is the foundation of mindfulness?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna—leading to liberation, leading to the waning of existence, and directed away from views—
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge, contemplating phenomena in phenomena.
At that time, whatever mindfulness there is—recollection, right mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, a factor of the path, included within the path—that is [mindfulness].
This is called "the establishment of mindfulness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the establishment of mindfulness.
There are four establishments of mindfulness:

Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, and he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction of the acquisitions, [freeing him] from views...
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual desires...
[as before] ...one enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge. At that time, there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
As a result of having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna,
he, secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge,
and is empty; wherein at that time there is mindfulness, recollection, right mindfulness, the mindfulness enlightenment factor, a path constituent, included in the path— this is that.
This is called "the establishment of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
All remaining phenomena are associated with the establishment of mindfulness.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating feelings in feelings?

Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is emancipating, leading to the destruction of acquisitions, for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage—being secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge—at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
As a result of having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna, he—
quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice, slow in its direct knowledge, and empty.
Contemplating feelings in feelings: whatever at that time is mindfulness, recollection, right mindfulness, the mindfulness enlightenment factor,
a path factor included in the path—
this is called "the establishment of mindfulness."
The remaining phenomena are associated with the foundations of mindfulness.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the mind in the mind?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction [of the taints], free from views...
For the sake of abandoning [the defilements] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These phenomena are wholesome.
As a result of having performed and cultivated that same supramundane wholesome jhāna,
he, secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge,

and is empty; therein, when he is contemplating the mind as mind, whatever mindfulness there is— recollection, right mindfulness, the mindfulness enlightenment factor, the path factor, included in the path— that at that time [is present].
This is called "the establishment of mindfulness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the establishment of mindfulness.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena?

Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, leads to the abandoning of views, and leads to the destruction [of the taints], for the attainment of the first stage—secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge—at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
As the result of having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice, slow in its direct knowledge, and empty.
Contemplating phenomena in phenomena: whatever at that time is mindfulness, recollection, right mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness,
a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "the foundation of mindfulness."
The remaining phenomena are associated with the foundations of mindfulness.
Therein, what is the foundation of mindfulness?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation and results in the dismantling of the acquisitions of views—
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual desires...
[as before] ...one enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Due to having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna, he,
secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge,

and is empty. At that time, whatever mindfulness there is— mindfulness, recollection, right mindfulness, the mindfulness enlightenment factor, the path factor, included in the path— that is [the emptiness-enlightenment-factor].
This is called “the foundation of mindfulness.
The remaining phenomena are associated with the foundation of mindfulness.
This is the Analysis of the Abhidhamma.
3. Interrogation on Questions:

The Four Foundations of Mindfulness—here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

Of the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate? …pe… How many are with conflict (*saraṇa*), and how many are without conflict (*araṇa*)?
3.1. The Triads:
They may be wholesome, or they may be indeterminate …pe….
It may be associated with pleasant feeling; it may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
It may be resultant; it may be of a nature to produce resultants.
It is not acquired through clinging and is not conducive to clinging.
They are undefiled and not subject to defilement.

They may be accompanied by both initial and sustained application of thought, they may be without initial application and with sustained application only, or they may be without both initial and sustained application of thought.
They may be accompanied by rapture, they may be accompanied by pleasure, or they may be accompanied by equanimity.
Not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
Not having roots to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
They may be conducive to diminution, or they may be neither conducive to accumulation nor conducive to diminution.
They may be of those in training (sekha), or they may be of those beyond training (asekha).
They are immeasurable.
They have immeasurable objects.
Exalted.
It may be fixed in rightness, or it may be unfixed.

It does not have the Path as its object; it may have the Path as its cause, or it may have the Path as its predominance; or it may be such that it cannot be said to have the Path as its cause, nor can it be said to have the Path as its predominance.
They may have arisen, they may not have arisen, or they may be in the process of arising.
They may be past, they may be future, or they may be present.
They should not be described as having a past object, nor as having a future object, nor as having a present object.
They may be internal, they may be external, or they may be both internal and external.
They have external objects.
They are non-manifest and non-reactive.
3.2. The Dyads:
Those without roots;
those with roots.
Associated with causes.
They should not be described as both causes and accompanied by causes; rather, they are accompanied by causes but are not themselves causes.
They should not be described as both causes and associated with causes; rather, they are associated with causes but are not themselves causes.
They are not causes, yet they possess causes;
they have conditions;
they are conditioned.
Non-indicative.
Non-reactive.
Formless.
Supramundane.
Knowable by some, unknowable by others.
Not taints.
They are without taints. They are dissociated from the taints.
They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not taints."
They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not taints.
They are dissociated from taints; they are without taints (anāsava).
There are no fetters … [and so on] … no ties … [and so on] … no floods … [and so on].
There are no fetters … [and so on] … there are no hindrances … [and so on] … there are no misapprehensions … [and so on] …
They have an object.
They are not consciousness.
They are mental factors.
Associated with consciousness.
Conjoined with consciousness.
Generated by consciousness.
Co-existent with consciousness,
following after consciousness,
conjoined with and produced by consciousness.
Those conjoined with and produced by mind and co-existent with it;
those conjoined with and produced by mind and following after it;
and external [phenomena].
Without clinging. Not clung to.
Without grasping ... pe ...
There are no defilements ...
[as before] ... that are to be abandoned by vision, nor to be abandoned by cultivation.
There are none whose roots are to be abandoned by vision.
They have roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
They may be with initial application, or they may be without initial application.
They may be with sustained application, or they may be without sustained application.
It may be with zest, or it may be without zest.
It may be accompanied by rapture, or it may not be accompanied by rapture.
It may be accompanied by pleasure, or it may not be accompanied by pleasure.
It may be accompanied by equanimity; it may not be accompanied by equanimity.
It is not of the sense sphere;
it is not of the fine-material sphere.
They do not belong to the formless realm.
They are not included within the mundane.
They may be leading to liberation, or they may not be leading to liberation.
It may be determinate; it may be indeterminate.
It is unsurpassed.
It is without conflict.
The Section on Questioning.
The Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness is finished.
